text: A group is a record on sys_user_group — a Service Desk team, a department, anything you assign work to as a unit rather than to one named person. Just like sys_user is the source of truth for people, sys_user_group is the source of truth for teams.

When you look at a Group's Group Members list, or a User's Groups list, you're looking at two views into the same table: sys_user_grmember. It's a many-to-many join with a user field and a group field — one row per membership. The UI never makes you touch it directly, but scripts and reports do.

Groups matter because of Assignment group. An incident has two separate fields: Assignment group, pointing to a team, and Assigned to, pointing to one person. Work lands in a visible team queue before anyone claims it — so it doesn't get stuck with one person who's out, and managers can see workload at a glance.

Two more fields worth knowing: Group Email, a shared mailbox used when notifications target the whole group instead of one person, and Manager, a reference to the user who leads the group — used in approval routing and reporting.

Adding a member is a two-click job from either form — the Group's Group Members list, or the User's Groups list. Both write the same row in sys_user_grmember. Neither path is more correct; it's the same relational pattern you'll see again with roles.
Groups are how work actually gets routed as a team, not just to an individual. Next up: roles — how ServiceNow decides what a user is actually allowed to do once they're logged in.
